triage.name: Diabetes Type 1
triage.reason: Classic presentation with polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss and possible DKA; diagnosis reachable by history, labs and ketone assessment.

review_issues: exam: term 'Delayed capillary refill' not found in SNOMED CT

demographics: Higher incidence in non-Hispanic White and Northern European populations.

risk_factors.text: Personal history of another autoimmune disease (e.g., autoimmune thyroid disease, celiac disease)
History of certain viral infections (e.g., enterovirus)

family_history: Type 1 diabetes in a first-degree relative

chief_complaints.text: I am thirsty all the time
I have to pee constantly, including at night
I have lost weight without trying

hpi.onset: Often abrupt over days to weeks, especially in children; may be more gradual in adults.
hpi.duration: Symptoms typically present for 1–3 weeks before diagnosis; DKA can develop within days.
hpi.progression: Polyuria and polydipsia appear first, followed by fatigue, weight loss, and sometimes vomiting, abdominal pain, or altered mentation as DKA develops.
pertinent_negatives: Burning with urination or flank pain
History of pancreatitis or pancreatic surgery
Use of glucocorticoids or other hyperglycemic drugs

positives.text: Waking up at night to urinate

argues_against: Colicky flank pain radiating to the groin

atypical.how_it_differs: Onset is often abrupt with polyuria, polydipsia, and weight loss; DKA at diagnosis is common because parents may not recognize early signs.
May present with irritability, poor feeding, dehydration, and tachypnea from DKA; polyuria is often not noticed because of diapers, and failure to thrive may be the main sign.
May have slower onset, less weight loss, and be mistaken for type 2 diabetes initially; ketosis may be absent at first.
Symptoms can be attributed to normal pregnancy; DKA can occur at lower glucose levels and progress rapidly.
Obesity does not rule out type 1; patients may be misdiagnosed as type 2 because of body habitus and slower onset.

general.mild: Well-appearing; alert and interactive, may have mild dehydration but no respiratory distress.
general.moderate: Tired but responsive; signs of mild dehydration such as dry mouth and slightly reduced skin turgor.
general.severe: Ill-appearing and lethargic; deep, rapid (Kussmaul) respirations; pronounced dehydration with poor skin turgor and dry mucous membranes.
general.critical: Obtunded or comatose; hypovolemic shock with hypotension and poor perfusion; Kussmaul respirations may be present or breathing may become shallow as the patient tires.

findings.maneuver: Pinch skin on the forearm or abdomen and release.
Press on a nail bed until it blanches and release.
Inspect the neck, axillae, and flexural areas.
Inspect and palpate the thyroid gland.

labs.caveat: Random glucose ≥200 mg/dL with classic symptoms is diagnostic; fasting is not needed.
May be near normal in very acute onset; repeat if initially nondiagnostic.
Low when DKA is present; normal in mild hyperglycemia without acidosis.
Serum potassium may be normal or high from acidosis despite total-body depletion; recheck before giving insulin.
Hyperglycemia causes dilutional hyponatremia; correct sodium for glucose if needed.
Prerenal from osmotic diuresis and vomiting.
Compensatory respiratory alkalosis from Kussmaul respirations.
Glucosuria occurs when serum glucose exceeds the renal threshold (~180 mg/dL).
Positive in DKA; serum ketones are more accurate.

initial.why: Glucose, electrolytes, bicarbonate, and renal function; identifies hyperglycemia and screens for DKA.
Urine glucose and ketones support the diagnosis and screen for DKA.
Assess for infection and hemoconcentration in DKA.

initial.only_if: DKA is suspected (Kussmaul breathing, vomiting, altered mentation, positive urine ketones, or low bicarbonate on BMP)

confirmatory.why: Diagnostic criterion and baseline glycemic control.
Low or undetectable level indicates insulin deficiency and helps distinguish type 1 from type 2.
Most common autoantibody in type 1 diabetes; positive in most patients.
More common in children with recent-onset type 1 diabetes.
confirmatory.only_if: young child or very recent onset

confirmatory.why: Additional autoantibody; adds sensitivity when GAD65 is negative.
Additional autoantibody; adds sensitivity when other autoantibodies are negative.

supporting.why: Magnesium can fall after insulin therapy in DKA.
supporting.only_if: DKA and significant electrolyte depletion or symptoms

supporting.why: Phosphate can fall after insulin therapy in DKA.
supporting.only_if: DKA and significant electrolyte depletion or symptoms

supporting.why: Rules out pregnancy if pregnancy is possible.
supporting.only_if: adolescent or adult female with pregnancy possible

supporting.why: Screen for autoimmune thyroid disease, which commonly coexists with type 1 diabetes.
supporting.only_if: symptoms of thyroid dysfunction or goiter
potassium >5.5 mEq/L or DKA with severe hyperglycemia

not_indicated.why: No role unless abdominal pain suggests pancreatitis.
No role in diagnosing diabetes or DKA unless fever, hypoxia, or respiratory distress suggests pneumonia or aspiration.
No role in routine evaluation of new diabetes.
No role unless bacterial infection is suspected.
No role in diagnosing type 1 diabetes or DKA.

decision_points: Random glucose ≥200 mg/dL with classic symptoms is diagnostic; do not wait for fasting or A1C.
If DKA is suspected, start fluids and insulin promptly after labs; do not delay treatment for imaging.
In children with new-onset diabetes and moderate or severe DKA, arrange ICU admission and careful potassium replacement.
Pregnancy testing before any test or medication that could affect pregnancy, if relevant.

criteria.name: ADA diagnostic criteria for diabetes mellitus
criteria.summary: One of the following, confirmed by repeat testing unless unequivocal hyperglycemia
items: Fasting plasma glucose ≥126 mg/dL after at least 8 hours with no caloric intake
2-hour plasma glucose ≥200 mg/dL during a 75-g oral glucose tolerance test
Random plasma glucose ≥200 mg/dL with classic symptoms of hyperglycemia or hyperglycemic crisis

criteria.name: Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) diagnostic criteria
criteria.summary: All three of the following: hyperglycemia, ketosis, and high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis
items: Serum glucose usually >250 mg/dL (may be lower in pregnancy or SGLT2 inhibitor use)
pH <7.3 and/or serum bicarbonate <18 mmol/L with anion gap >12

differential.name: Type 2 diabetes
differential.why_considered: Polyuria, polydipsia, and elevated blood glucose occur in both types.

history: Insidious onset over months to years
History of gestational diabetes or metabolic syndrome
labs: A1C may be high but ketones usually negative

differential.name: Monogenic diabetes
differential.why_considered: Young age at diagnosis and strong family history can mimic type 1 diabetes.

history: Autosomal dominant family history of diabetes (multiple generations)

differential.name: Diabetes insipidus
differential.why_considered: Polyuria and polydipsia are the primary symptoms.

exam: No signs of dehydration if access to water
labs: Water deprivation test shows inability to concentrate urine
imaging: Brain MRI may show absent posterior pituitary bright spot in central DI

differential.name: Hyperthyroidism
differential.why_considered: Weight loss, fatigue, polyphagia, and increased thirst can overlap with type 1 diabetes.

differential.name: Addison disease
differential.why_considered: Fatigue, weight loss, abdominal pain, and vomiting can be seen; autoimmune adrenalitis may coexist with type 1 diabetes.
differential.trigger: Hypotension, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, hypoglycemia, or hyperpigmentation in a patient with fatigue and weight loss, especially if type 1 diabetes is present or suspected.

exam: Hyperpigmentation of skin creases, gums, or scars
labs: Hypoglycemia (in contrast to hyperglycemia in type 1 diabetes)
imaging: Adrenal CT may show small or enlarged adrenal glands depending on cause

severity.mild: New-onset hyperglycemia without significant dehydration or acidosis; patient is well-appearing, able to eat and drink.
severity.moderate: Hyperglycemia with mild dehydration and early ketosis; may have nausea, vomiting, and mild acidosis but no altered mental status.
severity.severe: DKA with moderate-to-severe dehydration, Kussmaul respirations, abdominal pain, and lethargy; pH <7.2 and serum bicarbonate <10 mmol/L.
severity.critical: Severe DKA with obtundation or coma, hypotension, or pH <6.9; immediate ICU care needed.

red_flags.meaning: DKA; requires immediate blood gas, ketone testing, and insulin/fluids
Cerebral edema or severe acidosis; immediate ICU
Severe DKA with volume depletion; aggressive fluid resuscitation
DKA can mimic acute abdomen; treat DKA first

complications.name: Hypoglycemia
clues: Occurs after insulin or missed meals

special_populations.differences: Onset is often abrupt with DKA at diagnosis; management requires pediatric-specific fluid and insulin protocols and ICU admission for moderate/severe DKA.
May present with failure to thrive, dehydration, and tachypnea from DKA; polyuria is often not noticed because of diapers; insulin dosing is especially challenging.
May have slower onset and be misclassified as type 2 diabetes; ketosis may be absent initially; lower threshold for evaluating autoimmune markers.
DKA can occur at lower glucose levels and progress rapidly; requires immediate obstetric and endocrine involvement; insulin requirements increase later in pregnancy.
Obesity does not exclude type 1; patients may be misdiagnosed as type 2 because of body habitus; consider autoantibody testing if clinical features suggest type 1.

key_questions.question: When did the thirst and frequent urination start, and how quickly have they gotten worse?
key_questions.looking_for: Days to weeks; abrupt onset in children

key_questions.question: Do you wake up at night to urinate, and how much are you drinking each day?
Have you lost weight without trying?
key_questions.looking_for: Unintentional weight loss despite increased appetite

key_questions.question: Have you felt more tired or hungry than usual?
Have you noticed any blurry vision?
key_questions.looking_for: Blurred vision from osmotic lens changes

key_questions.question: Have you had nausea, vomiting, or belly pain?
Have you noticed your breathing is deep or rapid, or a fruity smell on your breath?
Have you felt confused, very sleepy, or less alert than usual?
key_questions.looking_for: Altered mental status from DKA or cerebral edema

key_questions.question: Does anyone in your family have type 1 diabetes or another autoimmune disease?
key_questions.looking_for: Family history of type 1 or autoimmune disease

key_questions.question: Do you have any personal history of autoimmune disease, like thyroid or celiac disease?
Have you taken any steroids or other medications that can raise blood sugar?
Could you be pregnant?
key_questions.looking_for: Pregnancy; DKA can occur at lower glucose and affects management

reasoning_points: Polyuria, polydipsia, and unintentional weight loss are classic symptoms.
Random blood glucose ≥200 mg/dL with symptoms, or fasting ≥126 mg/dL or A1C ≥6.5%, confirms diabetes.
Low or undetectable C-peptide indicates insulin deficiency.
Positive islet autoantibodies (GAD65, IA-2, ZnT8, or IAA) confirm autoimmune type 1 diabetes.
Absence of features of type 2 diabetes (obesity, acanthosis nigricans, strong family history of type 2) supports type 1.
Evidence of DKA (ketones, anion-gap metabolic acidosis, Kussmaul respirations) supports type 1 and guides urgent management.
Normal glucose with low urine osmolality would point to diabetes insipidus, not type 1 diabetes.

easy: Child or adolescent with classic triad: polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss
Random glucose markedly elevated with glucosuria and ketones
No confounding features of type 2 diabetes
medium: Adult with slower onset and obesity, requiring autoantibody testing to distinguish from type 2
Moderate DKA with nausea, vomiting, and Kussmaul respirations
Young child with enuresis or recurrent infection as main complaint
hard: DKA with altered mental status or cerebral edema
Infant or toddler with failure to thrive and dehydration
Older adult misdiagnosed as type 2 with negative or weakly positive autoantibodies
